correctness.summary: For 0<lambda<2, each relaxed projector has an exact norm-decrease identity; positive definiteness of the sum of projectors makes every complete ordered product a strict contraction. Expanding the affine sweep through second order gives an analytic fixed-point branch with first-order coefficient S^{-1} sum_{p<q} P_{pi_q} r_{pi_p}. The least-squares residuals sum to zero and satisfy P_i r_i=r_i, which makes the reverse-order coefficient the negative of the forward coefficient. The explicit scalar three-equation example verifies that the remaining midpoint term can be genuinely quadratic.

originality.scope: to the best of our knowledge
originality.summary: The 1983 strong-underrelaxation theorem establishes convergence of cyclic limit points to a weighted least-squares solution as lambda tends to zero. Later work develops exact least-squares extensions, block and randomized variants, and symmetric forward/backward Kaczmarz-SOR sweeps. Targeted searches did not locate the explicit first-order fixed-point bias formula or the theorem that averaging the fixed points of opposite cyclic orders cancels that bias. Generic forward/reverse averaging is known as a second-order symmetrization device in operator-splitting time integration, so novelty is not claimed for the abstract symmetrization idea itself. The full texts of Censor--Eggermont--Gordon (1983) and Popa (1995) were not inspected end-to-end, leaving residual coverage risk.

value.summary: The result converts the qualitative strong-underrelaxation limit into an explicit local error model, identifies exactly how row or block order enters the leading bias, and gives a simple order-reversal correction that improves asymptotic least-squares accuracy by one power of the relaxation parameter. It applies uniformly to ordinary and block orthogonal-projection Kaczmarz schemes and includes a sharpness example.

limitations: The sum of the projectors must be positive definite.
The second-order midpoint guarantee is asymptotic as lambda tends to zero.
No finite-lambda uniform constant, floating-point stability theorem, or solver-speed advantage is claimed.
The two cyclic fixed points must be resolved accurately enough that iteration error does not dominate the asymptotic bias.
The full text of Censor--Eggermont--Gordon (1983) was not inspected end-to-end; a hidden rate expansion or order-symmetrization statement there remains a residual originality risk.
The full text of Popa (1995) was not inspected; a specialized opposite-order construction there remains a residual originality risk.
Generic forward/reverse averaging is known in symmetrically weighted sequential operator splitting, so only the Kaczmarz fixed-point expansion and bias-cancellation statement are claimed here.
Independent audit has not been performed.
